title: Bold as a leopard (Avot 5:20)
hookLine: Yehuda ben Tema: bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, strong as a lion to do God's will
tomorrow: why read the same old text again and again?

cards: Some people can ask anyone for anything: a better seat, a refund, a second chance. Others would rather go without than ask. Plenty of people sit in between, rehearsing the request and never sending it.
So is it bold, or just rude, to ask for a favor? Avot has a sage who wants you fearless, and in the very next breath, the same sage warns against a face with no shame.

teach.b: Yehuda ben Tema says: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer and strong as a lion, to do the will of your Father in heaven.
Then he says: the brazen-faced are bound for Gehinnom; the shamefaced, for the Garden of Eden. Bold, and yet not brazen. Readers argue over that seam.
One side leans on the animals.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: DON'T BE SHAMED OUT OF DOING RIGHT.
teach.b: The Shulchan Aruch, a code of Jewish law, opens with this saying, and its first paragraph explains the leopard: don't be embarrassed before people who mock you for doing right.
On this view, shyness can keep good things from happening. Say the thing. Ask for the favor.

teach.h: OTHER SIDE: SHAME IS THE BRAKE.
teach.b: The other side leans on the next line. Shame isn't only a weakness here; it's what keeps boldness from turning into a face that can't blush. The Talmud names bashfulness as a mark of Abraham's children.
On this view, the leopard is only for the will of heaven, and the bold need a brake. The mishnah keeps both, side by side. A leopard for the good thing.
A face that can still blush while doing it.

how: The Shulchan Aruch opens with Yehuda ben Tema's saying, and some observant Jews take its lion as the call to get up in the morning for prayer; Avot 5:20 is studied with chapter five on summer Shabbat afternoons.

games.q: what does “bold as a leopard” mean?
o: a wild spirit that won't be tamed
daring to do right without being shamed
fierce in a fight and quick to strike

games.q: Yehuda ben Tema's four animals — tap the pairs.

s: the mishnah praises boldness in every situation
bold as a leopard, to do the will of heaven; the next line warns the brazen-faced.
the Shulchan Aruch, a code of Jewish law, opens with this saying
and explains the leopard: don't be embarrassed before people who mock you for doing right.

games.q: your friend says shyness is just a weakness to get rid of. make the best case for the other side, from this mishnah.
o: the same mishnah praises the shamefaced: a sense of shame keeps boldness from turning brazen.
shyness never comes up in Avot; only the four animals count as virtues.
boldness is for lions and leopards; people should simply stay modest.
games.why: Yehuda ben Tema wants the leopard's nerve for doing right, and in the next breath sends the brazen-faced to Gehinnom and the shamefaced to Eden. both sides are in one mishnah.

practice: Stand, if you can, feet planted, shoulders back, the way you'd stand before saying something hard. Name one good thing you've been too shy to do or ask, and say it once, out loud, in a plain voice.
Then soften your face, and keep standing for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Bold as a leopard: Yehuda ben Tema's first animal. Bold for doing right, and never brazen-faced.

carryVoice: The leopard, with a blush: bold as a leopard, for the good thing. Fifty-three days into Avot.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 79a (bashfulness as a mark of Abraham's descendants)
